In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

tmpfs: keep the quota soft limits of an unused id

When the last reference to a dquot goes away, shmem_release_dquot()
stores its limits in the rb tree of the mount, unless
shmem_is_empty_dquot() says that there is nothing worth storing. That
function looks at the usage and at the two hard limits only.

So if the administrator sets nothing but soft limits for an id that owns
no file yet, the entry is thrown away as soon as the dquot that
Q_SETQUOTA used is released, and the id never gets to see a limit.

To fix it, compare the soft limits as well: an entry can be empty only if
both soft limits are zero as well, which is exactly what
shmem_acquire_dquot() sets for a new entry.

Fix generated by an LLM and sent by Josef Bacik in private.

[ david: slightly adjusted description ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

mm/mempolicy: charge shared policy nodes

Any local user can bypass memory.max with mbind() on a tmpfs file, and
allocate unbounded kernel memory.

mbind() sets a NUMA memory policy for a range of a mapping. If the
mapping is of a shmem and friends, the kernel also stores the policy on
the inode, in a tree with one entry per range of the file.

Each mbind() on a single page of a mapping can add one shared policy node
(struct sp_node) and one struct mempolicy to that tree. They outlive the
mapping and stay around until the inode is destroyed. The tree is not
bounded by the file size, so the file can be empty.

Memory that user space can allocate must be charged to a memory cgroup. A
slab cache does that for all of its objects if it is created with
SLAB_ACCOUNT. numa_policy_init() creates the slab caches for both
structs without SLAB_ACCOUNT, so they are not charged to any cgroup.

Reproduced with mbind() on single pages of an empty tmpfs file, from a
cgroup with memory.max=8M: the global OOM killer killed tasks owned by
root, and the machine panicked.

Fix this by creating both caches with SLAB_ACCOUNT. This change implies
that mbind() can now fail when running into memcg limits. Further,
the policy_cache also serves task and VMA policies, so they are
similarly accounted now.

Note that per-file limits are not really helpful, as the user could
simply use many files; having limits per user is tricky as well.

Fix generated by an LLM and submitted by Chris Mason in private.

[ david: smaller description tweaks ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: grant a POSIX ACL group entry only to the group's members

When no ACE of the DACL matches the caller, Everyone or Authenticated
Users, smb_check_perm_dacl() falls back to the file's POSIX ACL. It
takes the first ACL_USER or ACL_GROUP entry whose id equals the
caller's uid. For ACL_GROUP, this compares a gid with the caller's uid.
A numerical match grants the group's permissions even when the caller
is not a member.

Match a group entry only when the caller is also in the group.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net: atl1c: drop oversized RX frames instead of panicking

atl1c sizes its receive buffers from the netdev MTU plus a fixed set of L2
overheads, which comes to 1522 bytes at the default MTU.  A link partner
that sends a longer frame - in practice a MikroTik CCR2004-1G-2XS-PCIe,
whose RouterOS side defaults to l2mtu 1600 while the host stays at MTU 1500
- makes the length reported by the RX return descriptor exceed what the
hardware wrote, and skb_put() then either includes bytes that were never
received or trips skb_over_panic and takes the host down.

Compare the descriptor length against buffer_info->length, the length the
hardware was given, rather than against skb_tailroom(): the skb carries 64
bytes of slack for the DMA erratum, so tailroom is larger than the DMA
buffer and a frame in between would pass the check and still be delivered
with a tail the device never wrote.  The same test rejects frames shorter
than ETH_HLEN + ETH_FCS_LEN; before this change a reported length below
ETH_FCS_LEN underflowed in skb_put().

The frame is dropped with kfree_skb_reason(SKB_DROP_REASON_PKT_TOO_BIG) so
drop_monitor and the kfree_skb tracepoint see it, and counted through
dev_core_stats_rx_dropped_inc(), which survives atl1c_get_stats()
overwriting the hardware counters on every read.  It also counts as work:
atl1c_clean_rfd() has already recycled the RFD, and the refill at the end
of the poll only runs when work_done is non-zero, so sustained oversized
traffic would otherwise drain the ring and stop RX.

Tested on a MikroTik CCR2004-1G-2XS-PCIe (4x AR8151) in a Proxmox VE host,
with atl1c built from a DKMS tree carrying this change: the l2mtu-1600
traffic that panics the stock driver is dropped and counted with the patch
applied, and received normally once the host MTU is raised to match.

This complements commit 36c2009d90f2 ("net: atl1c: fix soft lockup on
out-of-range tpd_cons read"), which fixed the TX side of the same
"host dies while the card resets" problem.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

x86/bugs: Select the BHI mitigation based on the attack vector properly

The BHI mitigation selection is inconsistent with the documentation
(attack_vector_controls.rst), which lists BHI under both the
user->kernel and guest->host attack vectors. bhi_select_mitigation()
only enables it when CPU_MITIGATE_GUEST_HOST is set; otherwise it
selects BHI_MITIGATION_OFF, even if CPU_MITIGATE_USER_KERNEL is set.

As a result, a kernel compiled with KVM disabled gets BHI automatically
disabled, since CPU_MITIGATE_GUEST_HOST defaults to off without KVM.
This is a bug, given that CPU_MITIGATE_USER_KERNEL still needs it: on
affected Intel CPUs these kernels lose BHI_DIS_S or the BHB clearing
loop by default. Booting with mitigations=auto,no_guest_host has the
same effect.

Select BHI_MITIGATION_ON whenever user->kernel is mitigated, and keep
BHI_MITIGATION_VMEXIT_ONLY for the guest->host-only case.

  [ bp: Clarify commit title. ]

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ASoC: SOF: Intel: hda-sdw-bpt: Stop active DMA before closing BPT streams

When sdw_enable_stream() fails in intel_ace2x_bpt_send_async() after
hda_sdw_bpt_send_async() has already started the TX and RX DMA streams,
intel_ace2x_bpt_close_stream() invokes hda_sdw_bpt_close() directly
without calling hda_sdw_bpt_wait().  As a result,
hda_sdw_bpt_dma_deprepare() tears down the DMA buffers and BDL while
the DMA hardware is still running.

Disable any running TX or RX BPT DMA stream at the start of
hda_sdw_bpt_close() before unmapping channels and depreparing DMA
resources.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: fix NULL pointer dereference in session_user_name() and session_account_type()

session_user_name() and session_account_type() dereference
session->user without checking for NULL. A session can be published
and exposed via the procfs session interface before authentication
completes, during which session->user is NULL:

  show_proc_session() -> session_user_name(sess)
    -> user_guest(session->user) -> NULL->flags -> oops

Guard both functions by treating a NULL session->user as an explicit
not-yet-authenticated state rather than dereferencing it.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: revert fsids on durable reconnect and replay failure

On a durable handle reconnect or a request replay, smb2_open() switches
to the SMB user's fsids before calling ksmbd_vfs_getattr(). If that call
fails, the code jumps to err_out2 and skips ksmbd_revert_fsids() at
err_out1. The user's credentials then stay installed on the shared ksmbd
worker. Later work on that worker, including other users' requests, runs
with the first user's fsuid, fsgid and supplementary groups.
ksmbd_free_work_struct() also warns, because work->saved_cred is still
set.

Jump to err_out1 instead. No path is held at this point, so skipping the
path_put() at err_out is correct.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: enforce the read-only share flag when creating a stream

When a share is read-only, smb2_open() rejects opens that would create
or truncate a file. Creating a named stream on an existing file with
streams_xattr sets neither O_CREAT nor O_TRUNC, so it passes this check,
and smb2_set_stream_name_xattr() then creates the stream. On a Time
Machine share, opening a missing AFP_AfpInfo stream also writes one. A
user who can write a file at the filesystem level can therefore add
streams to it through a read-only share.

Do not create a stream or synthesize AFP_AfpInfo when the share is not
writable. Existing streams still open normally, and a missing stream
opened with FILE_OPEN still returns STATUS_OBJECT_NAME_NOT_FOUND.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ksmbd: require DELETE access for delete-on-close opens

smb2_open() accepts FILE_DELETE_ON_CLOSE on an existing file without
DELETE in DesiredAccess. When the request asks only for
FILE_READ_ATTRIBUTES or READ_CONTROL, it also skips inode_permission()
and the parent directory MAY_WRITE | MAY_EXEC check that delete-on-close
is meant to get. The file is then marked for deletion by a caller who
could not delete it.

The unlink happens later, in __ksmbd_inode_close(), when the last handle
on the inode is closed, and it runs with the credentials of that handle.
If the caller closes last, the unlink fails. If another user who can
write the parent directory, such as the file's owner, still has the file
open, the file is deleted when that user closes it. Until then new opens
of the file fail with STATUS_DELETE_PENDING. So a user with only search
permission on a directory can delete a file in it, or block opens of it,
while the owner has it open.

A MAXIMUM_ALLOWED open that also requests DELETE has the same problem.
The requested access is replaced with the maximal access, which does not
include DELETE when the caller cannot write the parent directory, and the
later permission checks are skipped as already done.

MS-FSA 2.1.5.1 requires an open with FILE_DELETE_ON_CLOSE and without
DELETE in DesiredAccess to fail with STATUS_INVALID_PARAMETER, and Samba
does the same. Add that check to the CreateOptions validation, using
the generic-mapped DesiredAccess so that GENERIC_ALL still qualifies.
This also refuses MAXIMUM_ALLOWED with FILE_DELETE_ON_CLOSE but no
explicit DELETE, as MS-FSA and Samba do. When MAXIMUM_ALLOWED is
requested with DELETE but the maximal access does not include DELETE,
fail with STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED. With DELETE requested, delete-on-close
opens go through the existing parent directory check.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

bpf: Fix skb_pull() BUG in __bpf_redirect_neigh()

The issue:
This is a follow-up to the short link-layer header fixes from Eric.
After vlan pop_eth, a privileged SCHED_ACT BPF program can call
bpf_skb_change_head(skb, 1, 0) and then bpf_redirect_neigh().

__bpf_redirect_neigh() calls skb_pull(skb, sizeof(*ethh)) after checking
only that mac_header < network_header.  Nothing verifies that the MAC
header is long enough, that it is linear, or that the IP header the
redirect goes on to read is linear either.

A SCHED_ACT BPF program can do:

    bpf_skb_change_head(skb, 1, 0);
    bpf_redirect_neigh(lo, NULL, 0, 0);

after vlan pop_eth.  The skb then has mac_len == 1 and only one byte of
linear data; skb_pull(ETH_HLEN) trips the skb->len < skb->data_len BUG in
__skb_pull():

    kernel BUG at ./include/linux/skbuff.h:2839!
    RIP: skb_pull+0x40/0x50
    Call Trace: skb_do_redirect -> packet_xmit -> packet_sendmsg
    Kernel panic - not syncing: Fatal exception in interrupt

The v4 and v6 paths read ip_hdr() and ipv6_hdr() as soon as the MAC
header is gone.  On the AF_PACKET frame below that leaves headlen == 0
after the pull, so the network header sits at skb->tail and the route
lookup reads ip4h->protocol, ip4h->saddr and ip4h->daddr past the linear
area.

The Fix:
Use skb_network_offset(), which is the MAC header span, instead of
skb->mac_len.  mac_len is zero for locally generated tc egress and netkit
packets, while the span still rejects the one-byte header produced by
pop_eth + bpf_skb_change_head(skb, 1, 0).  The single check also covers
the mac_header >= network_header test it replaces.

Use pskb_may_pull() to make the Ethernet header linear before it is read
or pulled, and to make the IP header linear in both the v4 and the v6
path before ip_hdr()/ipv6_hdr() is read.  The header pointers are taken
after the pull, since pskb_may_pull() may reallocate skb->head.

Conditions to recreate the bug:
On x86-64 with 4 KiB pages, enable CONFIG_PACKET, CONFIG_BPF_SYSCALL,
CONFIG_NET_SCH_INGRESS, CONFIG_NET_CLS_MATCHALL, CONFIG_NET_ACT_VLAN and
CONFIG_NET_ACT_BPF.  Run as root with BPF loading, network administration
and raw-packet privileges.  Bring lo up and attach a SCHED_ACT program
that calls bpf_skb_change_head(skb, 1, 0), then returns
bpf_redirect_neigh(skb->ifindex, NULL, 0, 0):

  ip link set lo up
  tc qdisc add dev lo clsact
  tc filter add dev lo egress matchall action vlan pop_eth pipe \
      action bpf object-file neigh_chghead.o section action

Send an untagged ETH_P_IP frame of ETH_HLEN + 8192 bytes through an
AF_PACKET/SOCK_RAW socket bound to lo, without PACKET_VNET_HDR or
PACKET_QDISC_BYPASS.  Use a unicast destination MAC.  The sender's skb
has a 14-byte linear Ethernet prefix and a fragmented payload; pop_eth
removes that prefix and change_head restores only one linear byte.
The unfixed neighbor redirect then tries to pull 14 bytes and BUGs.

Sending the same frame without pop_eth and change_head leaves the IP
header in the frags, which is the route lookup reading past skb->tail.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/loongson: Handle buffer mapping failures when clearing a BO

lsdc_bo_clear() ignores the return value from lsdc_bo_kmap() and writes
to lbo->kptr unconditionally. When the first mapping of a newly allocated
buffer fails, kptr is still NULL and the subsequent memset accesses it.

Return the mapping error without touching the buffer and propagate it
from lsdc_gem_object_create(). Install the GEM object functions before
clearing so that drm_gem_object_put() can release the buffer correctly
on failure. Do not add the failed object to the tracking list or return
an uncleared buffer to the caller.

Imported buffers still skip clearing, and successfully mapped buffers
are cleared and unmapped as before.

Tested on LS7A2000 with a one-shot range error in ttm_bo_kmap(). Its
-EINVAL return reached userspace, the object was destroyed once, and
no GEM handle was published. Normal create/map/zero/write/read/close
cycles passed, with the tracked BO count and VRAM usage unchanged.

AI assistance was used for the lifetime analysis, fix, fault-injection
tools, build and test execution.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/loongson: Fix double free on BO initialization failure

If ttm_bo_init_validate() fails, it drops the buffer object's reference
and cleans it up through the supplied destroy callback. lsdc_bo_destroy()
releases the GEM object and frees the enclosing lsdc_bo, so freeing it
again in lsdc_bo_create() causes a double free on a synchronous failure
path.

Let TTM own the cleanup after initialization has started and return the
error directly. Keep the explicit free on drm_gem_object_init() failure,
which occurs before ownership is passed to TTM.

Tested on LS7A2000 by making drm_vma_offset_add() return -ENOSPC for one
selected dumb-buffer creation. The error reached userspace, the destroy
callback ran once, and no handle was published or tracked BO retained.
Normal buffer creation, zeroing, mapping, readback and release passed.

AI assistance was used for the ownership analysis, fix, fault-injection
tools, build and test execution.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

scsi: target: Verify the iSCSI ISID is null-terminated

iscsi_parse_pr_out_transport_id() returns the ISID of a FORMAT CODE 01b
TransportID as a pointer into the PERSISTENT RESERVE OUT parameter list,
lowercased in place and never null-terminated.  spc4r37 Table 508 requires
the field to be null-terminated, but a non-conforming initiator can omit
the NULL; when the ISID ends at the end of the received buffer, the pointer
is not a C string.

The registration code still consumes it as one: strcmp() in
__core_scsi3_locate_pr_reg() and in the REGISTER AND MOVE path, and
snprintf("%s") in __core_scsi3_do_alloc_registration(), which also reads
its first 8 bytes unconditionally with get_unaligned_be64() - a NUL check
does not bound that read.

When the parameter list spans more than one page, transport_kmap_data_sg()
maps it with vmap(), and the over-read walks off the end of the mapping
into the vmalloc() guard page and oopses.  Reproduced with a PR OUT
REGISTER + SPEC_I_PT parameter list of exactly 8192 bytes whose final
TransportID carries a 12-byte ISID without a terminating NUL:

  BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: ffffc9000138c000
  RIP: 0010:strcmp+0xc/0x30
  Call Trace:
   __core_scsi3_locate_pr_reg+0xd3/0x120 [target_core_mod]
   core_scsi3_decode_spec_i_port+0x8fc/0x13a0 [target_core_mod]
   core_scsi3_emulate_pro_register+0x73c/0x900 [target_core_mod]
   ...
   iscsi_target_rx_thread+0xef/0x1d0 [iscsi_target_mod]

With a single-page parameter list the buffer is a kmap() direct mapping, so
the over-read continues into the physically adjacent page instead of
faulting.  snprintf("%s") then copies whatever follows the ISID in memory
into pr_reg_isid, and PR IN READ FULL STATUS reports the registration back
to any initiator, turning the over-read into an info leak of kernel heap
contents.  Reproduced with a 4096-byte parameter list whose last
TransportID ends at the end of the buffer with a 4-byte ISID and no NUL,
interleaved with I/O to populate adjacent pages: the READ FULL STATUS
response returned the ISID as "0xleak" followed by raw bytes that were not
part of the parameter list.  The snprintf() into
pr_reg_isid[PR_REG_ISID_LEN] caps the echoed ISID at 15 characters, so at
most 11 bytes past the buffer are leaked per command, but the PR OUT
command is not rate limited.

Any initiator that can send PR OUT to an iSCSI-exported LUN can trigger
either variant, including a guest via vhost-scsi.

Require 8 bytes to remain after the ",i,0x" separator, and a NUL inside the
rest of the descriptor, before the ISID pointer is returned.  REGISTER AND
MOVE fails with TCM_INVALID_PARAMETER_LIST; on SPEC_I_PT no target port
claims the malformed TransportID, and the command fails the same way.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ptp: fix use-after-free in extts_fifo_show() reading tsevqs unlocked

extts_fifo_show() walks ptp->tsevqs with list_count_nodes() and then
list_first_entry() without holding ptp->tsevqs_lock, the spinlock that
"protects tsevqs from concurrent access". Every other accessor of the
list honours it: ptp_open() (list_add_tail), ptp_release() (list_del
followed by kfree of the per-fd queue), ptp_clock_release() and
ptp_clock_event() all take tsevqs_lock. extts_fifo_show() is the only
one that does not.

A per-fd timestamp queue is appended to tsevqs on open("/dev/ptpN") and
removed and freed on close(), both under tsevqs_lock:

	scoped_guard(spinlock_irq, &ptp->tsevqs_lock)
		list_del(&queue->qlist);
	bitmap_free(queue->mask);
	kfree(queue);

So a read of /sys/class/ptp/ptpN/fifo running concurrently with a
close() of a /dev/ptpN fd can have list_count_nodes() walk into the
queue that close() is removing and freeing, dereferencing freed memory
(use-after-free) or a poisoned list pointer.

Take tsevqs_lock around the list walk. The fifo only ever draws from the
first queue, which is the registration-time queue created in
ptp_clock_register() and freed only in ptp_clock_release(); that cannot
run while the sysfs attribute is being read, so the dequeue from
queue->buf under queue->lock may stay outside tsevqs_lock and the lock
order is unchanged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

btrfs: prevent deleting the wrong subvolume by ID

When deleting a subvolume by ID, btrfs_ioctl_snap_destroy() first
resolves the requested ID to a name, then looks up that name again
under the parent directory lock.

A concurrent rename can change which subvolume is associated with
the name between these operations. Since the deletion path does not
verify the ID of the resolved subvolume, it can delete a different
subvolume while leaving the requested one intact.

This was reproduced by repeatedly exchanging the names of two
subvolumes using renameat2(RENAME_EXCHANGE) while deleting one of
them by ID. The wrong subvolume was deleted in 9 out of 14 independent
tests.

Fix this by checking that the resolved subvolume ID matches the
requested ID while holding the parent directory lock. Return -EAGAIN
on a mismatch so that userspace can retry the operation instead of
being told that the requested subvolume does not exist.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

btrfs: sysfs: restore NOFS context on early return in btrfs_sysfs_add_block_group_type()

btrfs_sysfs_add_block_group_type() sets up a NOFS context with
memalloc_nofs_save() because kobject_add() performs GFP_KERNEL
allocations deep in its call chain, and the function may be called
while holding a transaction handle or a lock required for a
transaction commit, where reclaim could deadlock.

Every other return path of this function calls memalloc_nofs_restore()
except the early return taken when another thread has already created
the kobject for the same raid index (this can happen when restriping).
Taking that path leaves PF_MEMALLOC_NOFS set on the calling task, so
all subsequent memory allocations performed by that task remain
restricted to the NOFS scope, which may lead to unexpected allocation
failures or deadlocks later on.

Restore the NOFS context before returning from that path.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

sctp: account for chunk padding in sctp_init_cause()

sctp_init_cause() accepts a chunk when skb_tailroom() can hold the
cause header and the payload. sctp_addto_chunk() then writes 0-3
bytes of padding before that header so the chunk stays 4-byte
aligned. The check does not include the padding, and the following
skb_put() calls skb_over_panic() from softirq.

Count the padding sctp_addto_chunk() is about to write. The cause
length on the wire stays the header plus the payload.

Found by LLM inspection, triggered and tested the fix.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: tt: don't drop local events queued during TVLV update

batadv_tt_tvlv_container_update() read the number of local changes without
holding changes_list_lock. batadv_tt_local_event() is not serialized by
the commit_lock and can queue new events before the changes_list is
flushed:

  CPU0                          CPU1
  batadv_tt_tvlv_container_update()
    num = ...local_changes;
                                batadv_tt_local_event()
                                  list_add_tail(...);
                                  ...local_changes++;
    spin_lock_bh(&...changes_list_lock);
    /* only num events copied but all freed */

The additional events were freed without ever being sent. Other nodes will
only notice this via a CRC mismatch and must request the full table.

The number of changes and the changes_list must therefore be taken
atomically. Events queued afterwards then stay in the tt.changes_list for
the next TT round.

The changes can no longer be kept for the next round when the TVLV buffer
allocation fails. But they would be sent with a skipped TTVN anyway, so the
other nodes have to request the full table in this case either way. The
last changeset is only dropped in this case when the TTVN was incremented.
Without new changes, it still describes the current TTVN.

Previously, the unconsumed changes caused a retry of the TVLV container
update in the next commit round. Since the changes are now consumed, the
next round would only take the path without changes and wait for
BATADV_TT_OGM_APPEND_MAX rounds before updating the container again. Until
then, the outdated container with the previous TTVN would still be
announced. The ogm_append_cnt is therefore reset on failure to retry the
update in the next OGM interval.

This doesn't make the CRC consistent with the announced changeset. The
local table modifications are still not serialized with the commit and
batadv_tt_local_transition_new() can still make a client part of the CRC
for which the event is only part of the next TT round. Such an
inconsistency is detected by the CRC check of the other nodes and solved
via a full table request.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: tt: ignore ROAM flag of received ADD changes

A received TT change (OGM diff or full table response) with the ROAM flag
but without DEL is handled by batadv_tt_global_add() like a ROAMING_ADV:

* a newly created global entry gets BATADV_TT_CLIENT_ROAM and is
  therefore excluded from the global CRC. The sender has it in its local
  CRC and the receiver has to request the full table again
* batadv_tt_global_purge_local() removes the local entry of the
  receiver. The receiver's own client is considered as roamed to the sender
  and frames for it are rerouted

The ROAM flag only has a meaning together with DEL. Drop it on reception to
keep it from populating the global table with a temporary ROAMING entry
which is not part of the CRC - and therefore causing a CRC mismatch.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: stop originator purge worker before freeing TT

batadv_mesh_free() releases the translation tables via batadv_tt_free()
before batadv_originator_free() stops orig_work. The purge worker can
therefore still run while the TT is torn down. When an originator times
out, batadv_purge_orig_ref() calls batadv_tt_global_del_orig(), which
loads tt.global_hash and walks all buckets while taking their locks:

  CPU0                          CPU1
  batadv_tt_free()              batadv_purge_orig()
                                  batadv_tt_global_del_orig()
                                    hash = ...tt.global_hash;
    batadv_tt_global_table_free()
      batadv_hash_destroy(hash);
                                    spin_lock_bh(&hash->list_locks[i]);

Disable orig_work at the beginning of batadv_mesh_free(), directly after
the mesh was marked as deactivating. The second
disable_delayed_work_sync() in batadv_originator_free() is harmless because
it is free'd anyway.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

batman-adv: mcast: validate tracker padding before forwarding

A multicast tracker with an even number of destinations needs two
padding bytes after its destination list. batadv_mcast_forw_packet()
currently only checks that the count field and the addresses fit in
the tracker TVLV.

If an unpadded even tracker is compacted to an odd number of
destinations, batadv_mcast_forw_shrink_update_headers() includes those
missing padding bytes in the amount to remove. The subsequent memmove
can then write two bytes past the old packet tail. With no tailroom,
this corrupts skb_shared_info.

Include the required padding in the existing tracker length check.
This rejects the malformed tracker before either received or locally
generated packets can reach the compactor.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

9p: don't decrement a server-owned zero nlink

A 9P2000.L server can report nlink=0 for a regular file that still
exists.  On a cache=loose or cache=fscache mount, lookup stores that
value with set_nlink().  A later successful unlink calls
v9fs_dec_count(), which still calls drop_nlink() for a non-directory.
drop_nlink() warns, and the unsigned link count wraps to 4294967295.
fstat() on a descriptor opened before the unlink shows 0 before and
4294967295 after.

The warning on the unpatched kernel, trimmed:

WARNING: fs/inode.c:408 at drop_nlink+0xac/0xd0, CPU#1: trigger/188
CPU: 1 UID: 0 PID: 188 Comm: trigger Tainted: G                 N  7.3.0-rc4-00537-ga3ff15db6820 #1 PREEMPT(lazy)
RIP: 0010:drop_nlink+0xac/0xd0
Call Trace:
 <TASK>
 v9fs_remove+0x529/0x750
 vfs_unlink+0x2f0/0xbd0
 filename_unlinkat+0x340/0x6c0
 __x64_sys_unlink+0x46/0x70
 do_syscall_64+0xe8/0x4f0
 entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe+0x77/0x7f
 </TASK>
---[ end trace 0000000000000000 ]---

Directories whose cached nlink is at most 2 already skip this
decrement, because the exported filesystem may not maintain nlink
(commit ac89b2ef9b559).  cache=none skips it as well (commit
574aa0b479947).  cache=mmap does not take this path: it sets neither
CACHE_META nor CACHE_LOOSE.  A regular file on cache=loose or
cache=fscache still does.  Its count came from GETATTR and may
already be zero, so skip the decrement when i_nlink is already 0.

Verified on 7.3-rc4-00537-ga3ff15db6820 with only this change.  A
server that advertises nlink=0 and accepts the unlink no longer
warns, and the open descriptor stays at nlink 0.  An honest server
on the same mount still goes from 1 to 0.  A rejected unlink leaves
the count unchanged.  cache=none is unchanged.  With panic_on_warn
the unpatched kernel panics on the warning; the patched kernel does
not.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

9p/xen: validate the response size from the backend

p9_xen_response() takes the length of an incoming response from the ring
-- the first field of the 9p header, which the Xen transport reuses as
its framing header -- and uses it to advance the consumer index, but
never checks that it is at least the header size or no larger than the
number of bytes the backend has actually produced.

A malicious or buggy backend can post a response whose size is smaller
than the header (for example 0). The consumer index then never advances,
so the response work re-reads the same ring contents instead of making
progress. In testing this raced with the teardown that the malformed
reply triggers and dereferenced a freed p9_client:

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

scsi: target: Fix demo-mode dynamic ACL dev-entry UAF vs LUN teardown

A demo-mode (generate_node_acls=1) login that allocates a dynamic NodeACL
populates that ACL's per-LUN dev entries in core_tpg_add_node_to_devs()
*before* the ACL is linked onto tpg->acl_node_list by
target_add_node_acl():

	core_tpg_check_initiator_node_acl():
		...
		core_tpg_add_node_to_devs(acl, tpg, NULL); /* builds deves */
		target_add_node_acl(acl);                  /* only now listed */

The LUN teardown sweep, core_clear_lun_from_tpg(), enumerates only
tpg->acl_node_list, so a dev entry whose ACL is still in the window above
is invisible to the sweep and is never disabled.  It is left on the
se_lun->lun_deve_list after core_tpg_remove_lun() frees the se_lun; when
the same unpacked_lun is later re-added and the se_lun is reallocated at
the same address, the stale dev entry is rediscovered by
target_nacl_find_deve() and core_enable_device_list_for_node() corrupts
lun_deve_list:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free ...
   core_enable_device_list_for_node+0x5ce/0x880
   core_tpg_add_node_to_devs+0x169/0x190
   core_dev_add_lun+0x146/0x190
   target_fabric_port_link+0xe9/0x1b0
   configfs_symlink+0x381/0xae0
   __x64_sys_symlink+0x55/0x80

The demo-mode login path that drives the ACL/dev-entry creation is
reachable by an unauthenticated initiator; the colliding LUN add/remove is
a local configfs operation.

Commit 49cb77e297dc ("target: Avoid mappedlun symlink creation during lun
shutdown") introduced se_lun->lun_shutdown and guarded the *explicit* ACL
MappedLUN path (target_fabric_mappedlun_link()), but the demo-mode
automatic path, core_tpg_add_node_to_devs() ->
core_enable_device_list_for_node(), was never given the equivalent guard,
and the publish-after-populate ordering in
core_tpg_check_initiator_node_acl() was left unchanged.

Fix it in three cooperating parts:

 1) Publish the dynamic NodeACL onto acl_node_list *before* creating its
    dev entries, so the teardown sweep can observe them.

 2) Refuse to attach a dev entry to an se_lun that is shutting down,
    checked under nacl->lun_entry_mutex -- the same lock the sweep takes --
    so once the sweep has passed an ACL any later enable for that LUN
    observes lun_shutdown and skips it.

 3) In core_enable_device_list_for_node(), insert the new dev entry onto
    lun->lun_deve_list while still holding nacl->lun_entry_mutex, in both
    the replace and the new-entry branch.  Previously the entry was added
    to nacl->lun_entry_hlist under the mutex but to lun->lun_deve_list only
    after dropping it; with the ACL now published early, the sweep could
    take the mutex in that gap, find the entry on the hlist,
    core_disable_device_list_for_node() it (list_del() on the not-yet-
    linked lun_link succeeds and the entry is freed), and then the enable
    would list_add_tail() the freed entry back onto lun_deve_list.  Linking
    both lists under the mutex makes enable and the sweep mutually
    exclusive, closing that window.

core_tpg_add_node_to_devs() already ignores the return value of
core_enable_device_list_for_node(), so a shutting-down LUN is simply
skipped.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

scsi: aic79xx: Fix NULL pointer dereference in device reset

Since commit c67e63800446 ("scsi: aic79xx: Do not reference SCSI command
when resetting device") the device reset SCB has no SCSI command, but
ahd_linux_dev_reset() still sets its residual, and ahd_abort_scbs(), which
completes it, sets its status. Seen on an AIC-7902 when a failing disk
triggered a device reset, which killed the SCSI error handler:

  BUG: kernel NULL pointer dereference, address: 0000009c
  EIP: ahd_linux_dev_reset.cold+0xee/0x26e

Add NULL command checks to the accessors in aic79xx_osm.h. Also skip
autosense for an SCB without a command and complete it with ahd_done()
right away: the REQUEST SENSE path can clear SCB_DEVICE_RESET, after which
ahd_done() would dereference the missing command.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfrm4: use a full socket for local errors

xfrm4_local_error() passes skb->sk to inet_sk() and ip_local_error()
without ensuring it points to a full socket. TCP SYN-ACK skbs can be owned
by TCP_NEW_SYN_RECV request sockets.

xfrm4_tunnel_check_size() already checks sk_fullsock() since commit
1620c88887b1 ("xfrm: Fix the usage of skb->sk"), so iptfs_is_too_big() is
the only remaining IPv4 caller passing a request socket here: the sk it
tests is the listener, while skb->sk is the request socket.

When IP-TFS rejects such an skb because it exceeds its payload MTU, the
local error path treats the request socket as a struct inet_sock. KASAN
reports a slab-out-of-bounds read in ip_local_error() beyond the
request_sock_TCP allocation.

Resolve the skb owner with skb_to_full_sk() before accessing inet_sock
state or reporting the error. This maps a request socket to its listener
and rejects sockets that cannot be used as full sockets, matching what
commit 6973a21ee73c ("ipv6: xfrm: use full sockets in local error paths")
did for xfrm6_local_error().

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: mac80211: reinstate IEEE80211_TX_CTL_AMPDU flag in ieee80211_tx_prep_agg()

The commit 592234e941f1 ("wifi: mac80211: Fix iTXQ AMPDU fragmentation
handling") changed the way handling of the IEEE80211_TX_CTL_AMPDU flag
is done in mac80211, so the only place it is set is in
ieee80211_tx_dequeue().

This means that any frames that are sent to the driver via drv_tx() will
no longer have the flag set. In particular, this affects packets going
through ieee80211_tx_pending(). Evan reported that this can result in
the ath9k driver failing to account such packets in its block ack
window, eventually overrunning the window and stalling TX.

Fix this by reinstating the flag in ieee80211_tx_prep_agg() when inside
a valid block ack window. This should be harmless for the TXQ path, and
will reinstate the previous behaviour for drivers that use the flag as a
signal to track the packet in the window.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/vc4: Drop the BO reservations outside of job_lock

vc4_queue_submit() calls drm_exec_fini() with job_lock held and interrupts
disabled. Besides unlocking the reservations, drm_exec_fini() frees the
object array with kvfree(), which asks for preemptible task context or a
non-NMI interrupt, and may reach might_sleep() through vfree().

Considering that an array that exceeds a page can take the vmalloc
fallback, call drm_exec_fini() once job_lock is dropped. The reservations
are then held across the job kick, which is harmless as nothing in the
completion path takes a BO reservation.

Note that vc4_attach_fences() has to stay inside the critical section, as
it walks exec, which the job done worker is free to release as soon as
job_lock is dropped.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/vc4: Publish the output fence outside of job_lock

job_lock is taken by the V3D interrupt handler, so nesting an IRQ-unsafe
lock under it creates an inversion. drm_syncobj_replace_fence() takes
drm_syncobj::lock, which other paths acquire with interrupts enabled. For
example, a thread interrupted while holding it blocks the handler on
job_lock, and the handler can only make progress once the submit path
releases job_lock, which it cannot do while waiting for drm_syncobj::lock.

This is reported by lockdep:

[  188.139076] ========================================================
[  188.139086] WARNING: possible irq lock inversion dependency detected
[  188.139096] 7.3.0-rc3-00067-gc4f3feeaf60f #67 Tainted: G         C
[  188.139108] --------------------------------------------------------
[  188.139116] swapper/0/0 just changed the state of lock:
[  188.139125] ffff0000054f8ff8 (&vc4->job_lock){-...}-{3:3}, at: vc4_irq+0xa8/0x28c [vc4]
[  188.139234] but this lock took another, HARDIRQ-unsafe lock in the past:
[  188.139242]  (&syncobj->lock){+.+.}-{3:3}
[  188.139256] and interrupts could create inverse lock ordering between them.
[  188.139267] other info that might help us debug this:
[  188.139275]  Possible interrupt unsafe locking scenario:
[  188.139284]        CPU0                    CPU1
[  188.139291]        ----                    ----
[  188.139299]   lock(&syncobj->lock);
[  188.139312]                                local_irq_disable();
[  188.139320]                                lock(&vc4->job_lock);
[  188.139335]                                lock(&syncobj->lock);
[  188.139350]   <Interrupt>
[  188.139358]     lock(&vc4->job_lock);
[  188.139372] *** DEADLOCK ***

Hand the fence over after job_lock is dropped. The job can complete and
drop exec->fence in that window, so take a reference first and publish
through the local pointer, as exec may already be gone.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

wifi: mac80211: reload TDLS header pointer after skb_linearize()

ieee80211_process_tdls_channel_switch() sets tf = skb->data before it
calls skb_linearize(), and reads tf->action_code afterwards.

ieee80211_rx_h_data() queues TDLS channel switch requests and
responses to the interface after pulling only
offsetof(struct ieee80211_tdls_data, u) bytes, so the skb can still be
non-linear when the interface work handles it. Drivers that build
paged RX skbs do this for every frame that does not fit into the skb
head, e.g. iwlwifi (mvm), which is also the only mac80211 driver
that sets NL80211_FEATURE_TDLS_CHANNEL_SWITCH. If the remaining data
does not fit into the tailroom, skb_linearize() moves the data to a
new head and frees the old one, and the action code is then read from
freed memory. Depending on what that memory holds by then, the frame
is handled as before or ends in the WARN_ON_ONCE() of the default
case.

The frame only has to be a data frame with the TDLS ethertype from an
authorized peer, e.g. relayed by the AP from another station in the
BSS; the read happens before the sender is checked to be a TDLS peer.

Load tf after skb_linearize(), as the request and response handlers
already do.

Found by static analysis tool CodeQL.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/drm_crtc: fix race with dma_fence_signal() in ::get_driver_name()

Since commit 541c8f2468b9 ("dma-buf: detach fence ops on signal v3"),
I'm seeing the BUG_ON() triggering in drm_crtc's fence_to_crtc() via
drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name() regularly:

    Call trace:
     panic+0x58/0x5c
     die+0x160/0x178
     bug_brk_handler+0x70/0xa4
     call_el1_break_hook+0x3c/0x1a0
     do_el1_brk64+0x24/0x74
     el1_brk64+0x34/0x54
     el1h_64_sync_handler+0x80/0xfc
     el1h_64_sync+0x84/0x88
     drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name+0x60/0x68 (P)
     sync_file_get_name+0x184/0x45c
     sync_file_ioctl+0x404/0xf70
     __arm64_sys_ioctl+0x124/0x1dc

This looks to be caused by a code flow similar to the following:

+++ snip +++
thread A                             thread B

                                     ioctl(SYNC_IOC_FILE_INFO)
                                     sync_file_ioctl()
                                     sync_file_get_name()
dma_fence_signal_timestamp_locked()  dma_fence_driver_name()
                                       ops = rcu_dereference(fence->ops)
                                       if (!dma_fence_test_signaled_flag())
                                         ops->get_driver_name(fence) i.e.
                                         drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name()
test_and_set_bit(SIGNALED)
RCU_INIT_POINTER(fence->ops, NULL)
                                     drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name()
                                       BUG_ON(rcu_access_pointer(fence->ops)
                                              != &drm_crtc_fence_ops)
+++ snap +++

In other words, a fence's ops pointer can now change to NULL on signal,
which wasn't the case before the culprit commit and hence the BUG_ON()
triggers.

Simply drop the BUG_ON() as it's usage of fence ops is invalid now, and
because using BUG_ON() and friends to take down the system is an
unacceptable way to handle a failure.

Note that the adjacent drm_crtc_fence_get_timeline_name() has the same
problem and is fixed by this patch as well.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

drm/drm_crtc: ensure dma_fence_ops remain valid during device unbind

In [1], sashiko reported the following issue:

=== snip ===
Looking at how these fences are managed, drm_crtc_create_fence()
creates a dma_fence without taking a reference to the drm_device or
drm_crtc. Because the sync_file framework exposes this fence to
userspace, the fence can outlive the CRTC.

The dma_fence contract requires that data accessed by dma_fence_ops
(like get_driver_name) must remain valid for an RCU grace period after
the fence is signaled. However, drm_crtc_cleanup() and the subsequent
freeing of the device do not wait for an RCU grace period via
synchronize_rcu().

If userspace calls ioctl(SYNC_IOC_FILE_INFO) concurrently with a device
hot-unplug:

CPU1 (Userspace)
sync_file_get_name()
  ops = rcu_dereference(fence->ops);
  if (!dma_fence_test_signaled_flag())
    // Preempted or delayed here

CPU2 (Driver Teardown)
Signals the fence (setting fence->ops = NULL)
Destroys and frees the CRTC without waiting for an RCU grace period

CPU1 (Resumes)
  ops->get_driver_name(fence) -> drm_crtc_fence_get_driver_name()
  crtc = fence_to_crtc(fence); // Casts to the freed CRTC
  return crtc->dev->driver->name; // Use-after-free

...

Does the CRTC or DRM device need to be kept alive for the RCU grace
period, or should the fence hold a proper reference to prevent the
use-after-free when get_driver_name() and get_timeline_name() access
the freed CRTC structure?
=== snap ===

I believe this to be a correct observation and this patch implements
the suggestion of waiting for an RCU grace period before proceeding
with destruction of the drm_crtc, so that get_driver_name() and
get_timeline_name() can still work.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfrm: espintcp: reorder operations within espintcp_init_sk

When enabled on a socket, espintcp sets the socket callbacks to its
own before it has finished setting up its context and published it as
icsk_ulp_data. Any one of those callbacks that gets called before will
dereference a NULL icsk_ulp_data.

Fix this by reording the operations, and add memory barriers to ensure
callers will have a struct espintcp_ctx available. Add a few
WRITE_ONCE/READ_ONCE too while we're there.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfrm: interface: validate the IP header on xmit

Packets injected into an xfrm interface (e.g. AF_PACKET on an xfrmi
device) reach the xfrm output path without IP header validation, but
xfrm4_transport_output() uses iph->ihl for __skb_pull() and memmove()
and expects the header to be valid.

vti_tunnel_xmit() already calls pskb_inet_may_pull() before handing
packets to the xfrm output path.  Do the same in xfrmi_xmit() and
perform the header checks ip_rcv_core()/ip6_rcv_core() do on entry
to the IP stack: reject wrong IP versions and malformed IPv4 header
lengths.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/9p/usbg: clear stale client pointer on close

p9_usbg_close() tears down the client transport, but usb9pfs keeps
using usb9pfs->client from asynchronous TX and RX completion handlers.
A late completion can therefore dereference a client that has already
been freed during mount teardown.

Clear usb9pfs->client under usb9pfs->lock when closing the transport,
detach any pending TX request from in_req->context, and make the TX/RX
completion handlers bail out once the transport has been detached. This
keeps late completions from touching a freed or rebound p9_client.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/9p/usbg: remove bogus context initialization in alloc_requests

alloc_requests() initializes usb9pfs->in_req->context to point at the
struct f_usb9pfs instance itself. usb9pfs_queue_tx() later overwrites
this with the real struct p9_req_t pointer before every transmit, and
usb9pfs_tx_complete() clears it back to NULL after each completion, so
in_req->context only ever holds a valid p9_req_t once a request has
actually been queued.

usb9pfs_clear_tx(), however, can run at any time (mount close, gadget
disable) independent of whether a request was ever queued. If it runs
before the first usb9pfs_transmit(), it reads the leftover sentinel
value, type-confuses the struct f_usb9pfs pointer as a struct
p9_req_t, and both writes through it (req->t_err = -ECONNRESET) and
hands it to p9_client_cb(), which manipulates req->wq and req->refcount
at bogus offsets inside f_usb9pfs. This reliably corrupts memory or
panics whenever the transport is torn down before any 9p request has
been transmitted, e.g. mounting and immediately unmounting, or a cable
disconnect racing the very first request.

usb9pfs->out_req->context is set the same way but is never read by
this transport (usb9pfs_rx_complete() identifies the instance via
ep->driver_data instead), so it serves no purpose either.

Both endpoints' ->driver_data are already set to usb9pfs in
enable_endpoint(), which is what the completion handlers actually use
to recover the f_usb9pfs instance. Just drop the leftover
->context assignments; usb_ep_alloc_request()/alloc_ep_req() already
return zeroed requests, so in_req->context correctly starts out NULL.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/9p/usbg: fix out_req buffer leak in disable_usb9pfs

usb9pfs->out_req is allocated with alloc_ep_req(), which also
allocates the request's data buffer (req->buf). disable_usb9pfs()
frees it with plain usb_ep_free_request(), which only frees the
usb_request structure itself and leaks req->buf on every close.

Use free_ep_req() instead, matching the allocator, as documented by
its own comment ("Requests allocated via alloc_ep_req() *must* be
freed by free_ep_req()").

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/9p/usbg: call disable_usb9pfs() from usb9pfs_disable()

usb9pfs_disable() is the usb_function ->disable callback, invoked by
the composite gadget core whenever the host resets or unconfigures
the gadget. The gadget function API requires this callback to disable
its endpoints; every other in-tree function driver does so from its
->disable hook.

usb9pfs_disable() never called disable_usb9pfs(), so the IN/OUT
endpoints and their usb_request objects were left active and
allocated across a host-driven disable. When the host later
reconfigures the device, enable_usb9pfs() calls alloc_requests() again
and unconditionally overwrites usb9pfs->in_req/out_req, permanently
leaking the previous allocations, while the endpoints themselves are
left enabled underneath the function's own idea of being disabled.

Call disable_usb9pfs() before reinit_completion(&usb9pfs->send),
mirroring the same sequence already used in p9_usbg_close(). Placing
it before the reinit_completion() also ensures usb_ep_disable() has
synchronously flushed any requests still queued in hardware before the
completion is reset, closing the same race that motivated resetting
the completion here in the first place.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/9p/usbg: always reset completion when disconnecting

When some tx or rx transfers were pending while closing the connection,
the completion handler could catch one pending completion call. To
ensure a normal start when mounting again, we have to reset the
completion and flush any pending completions.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/9p/usbg: set client to Disconnected on usb9pfs_disable

This patch is setting the client status to Disconnected, when the
client is still in use. Otherwise a disconnected usb cable would run
any use of the mount to faults.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/9p/usbg: also disable endpoints on p9_usbg_close

The close function has to fully reverse the state change of 9p_create
(mount) and the potential call of set_alt(1). This includes to ensure
that the usage of the endpoints is not active any more.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

net/9p/usbg: Fix use-after-free in disable_usb9pfs()

disable_usb9pfs() frees the IN and OUT usb_request objects before it
disables the corresponding endpoints. If either request is still queued,
the later usb_ep_disable() call cancels the endpoint queue and the UDC
driver can still access the already freed request.

With dummy_hcd and KASAN, this is reproducible by queueing the OUT
request and then disconnecting the configfs gadget:

  BUG: KASAN: slab-use-after-free in dummy_disable+0x2b4/0x300
  Read of size 8 at addr ffff888009702400 by task sh/1
  usb_ep_disable+0x8e/0x1f0
  usb9pfs_func_unbind+0x193/0x350
  gadget_dev_desc_UDC_store+0x135/0x280

dummy_free_request() also warns because the request is freed while its
queue entry is still linked.

Disable both endpoints before freeing the request objects. This lets
usb_ep_disable() cancel any queued transfers and invoke the completion
callback while the request storage is still valid. The request objects
are then freed only after they have been removed from the endpoint
queues.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

9p/xen: fix refcount leak in p9_xen_response() on wrong tag

p9_xen_response() looks up the request for an incoming reply with
p9_tag_lookup(), which takes a reference on the returned p9_req_t. When
the tag does not resolve to a request in REQ_STATUS_SENT, the function
warns and continues the loop without dropping that reference, permanently
leaking the p9_req_t and its msize buffers. The reply header, including
the tag, is supplied by the backend, so a malicious or buggy 9P backend
can leak kernel memory on every crafted response.

Drop the reference before continuing.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

9p/trans_virtio: reject mount tags longer than NAME_MAX at probe

p9_virtio_probe() reads a 16-bit mount tag length (tag_len) from the
device config and kzalloc()s tag_len + 1 bytes for chan->tag with no
upper bound. A malicious or compromised host can present a tag of up to
65535 bytes; that tag is later copied into the single-page sysfs buffer
by p9_mount_tag_show() (memcpy(buf, chan->tag, tag_len + 1)), a
host-controlled out-of-bounds write of up to ~64 KiB past the PAGE_SIZE
attribute buffer.

Reject an overlong tag at probe time. A 9p mount tag is a name-like
identifier, so bound it by NAME_MAX (255): that limit is independent of
the sysfs/seq_file page size and is far above any legitimate mount tag,
which keeps p9_mount_tag_show() safe at the root without hard-coding a
seq_file implementation detail.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

xfrm: retry inexact policy lookup after node reinsertion

An inexact policy lookup first records pointers to candidate hlist heads
and then traverses the lists.  A concurrent policy insertion can merge
inexact tree nodes between those operations:

  lookup                         policy insertion
  ------                         ----------------
  find inexact candidates
    save obsolete hlist head
                                 write_seqcount_begin(&bin->count)
                                 merge inexact tree nodes
                                   hlist_del_rcu(&policy->bydst)
                                   reinsert policy->bydst in survivor
                                 write_seqcount_end(&bin->count)
  evaluate saved candidate list
    miss the moved policy

The merge immediately reinserts the same hlist node into the surviving
tree node.  RCU keeps the policy alive, but it does not provide a
consistent view while its list node is moved.  A lookup that selected the
obsolete list can observe it empty.  A lookup already traversing a moved
policy can instead follow the next pointer rewritten by the reinsertion.
Either case can return an incorrect IPsec policy result.

The per-bin sequence counter already brackets calls to
xfrm_policy_inexact_insert_node(), including node merges.  The read side,
however, currently validates the counter only while searching an
individual rb-tree.  A successful search returns without validation, and
the later candidate-list traversal is outside that read-side section.

Snapshot the per-bin sequence before discovering candidate heads and
validate it after evaluating all candidate lists.   Retry the lookup if
the inexact policy tree changes while it is being searched.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

cpufreq: CPPC: Select the frequency-invariance callback per CPU

cppc_cpufreq_cpu_fie_init() initializes deferred work only for CPUs whose
feedback counters use PCC. However, if any CPU in a shared policy uses PCC,
it installs the PCC tick callback for the entire policy. With FIE enabled,
a non-PCC CPU then queues an uninitialized irq_work and can call a NULL
function pointer when that work runs.

Choose the frequency-invariance callback separately for each CPU using
the recorded work-initialization state. Processor removal can unpublish
the CPC descriptor before callback registration, so querying its counter
transport again can incorrectly select direct reads for a PCC CPU.

Register the callbacks after all counter initialization has completed, so
a failed initial read for an online CPU cannot leave a partially
registered policy. PCC CPUs use their initialized deferred work, while
non-PCC CPUs read their own counters directly from the tick.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

ACPI: CPPC: Validate FFH register fields before hardware access

The x86 CPPC FFH accessors construct masks and shift values using the
firmware's Bit Width and Bit Offset without checking that the field fits
in an MSR. A zero-width field or a field extending beyond bit 63 can
therefore cause an invalid shift. The safe MSR accessors only handle an
access fault, not invalid field arithmetic after a successful read.

Also, the 64-bit GAS address is implicitly narrowed to the 32-bit MSR
number. A descriptor with nonzero upper address bits can access a different
MSR from the one described by firmware.

The arm64 AMU counter readers have the same unchecked field arithmetic.
Validate the field bounds before reading a counter, including both
descriptors in the paired counter path.

Dispatch FFH accesses before decoding the GAS Access Size in the common
read and write paths. Otherwise, a large access_width can trigger an
invalid shift in GET_BIT_WIDTH() before the architecture validates its
register. That field has architecture-specific FFH semantics and is not
needed by the generic memory/port accessor on this path.

Validate x86 MSR addresses and share the field-bounds checks between
related accessors within each architecture.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

block: restore the iterator when rejecting a misaligned bio

bio_iov_iter_get_pages() can extract some iovecs before encountering a
misaligned one.  It releases the pages and rejects the entire bio, but
leaves the supplied iterator advanced.

An iomap direct-I/O caller may subsequently reexpand the iterator's
byte count and fall back to buffered I/O.  The reexpanded count then
includes bytes before the iterator's current segment, potentially
causing iterate_iovec() to read beyond the imported iovec array.

In a reproducer using an initial empty iovec followed by 10-byte and
1015-byte segments, writev() returned 1015 instead of 1025 and KASAN
reported an 8-byte read beyond the nine-element iovec allocation.
Saving and restoring the iterator on the rejected-bio path makes
writev() return 1025 and eliminates the KASAN report.

Restore the entire iterator rather than reverting a byte count:
advancing past an empty segment changes its position without consuming
any bytes.

Leave successful and partially accepted bio paths unchanged.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

NFSD: stop registering with rpcbind after a failure in listener_set

nfsd_nl_listener_set_doit() calls svc_xprt_create_from_sa() once for each
requested listener and passes flags of 0, so every listener registers with
rpcbind on its own. A rpcbind that accepts the connection and never replies
therefore costs one timeout for each entry. With the cap of 1024 entries
the request can hold nfsd_mutex for about 34 minutes, which is roughly 17
times the hung-task threshold.

One failure is enough to know that the next call will not fare better.
Read svc_rpcb_failure_count() before the create loop, and pass
SVC_SOCK_ANONYMOUS for the rest of the request once the count moves.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

smb/server: prevent file publication after tree disconnect

TREE_DISCONNECT closes the tree's published file handles before marking and
removing the tree connection. A concurrent CREATE that already holds a tree
reference can therefore publish its file after the close pass. When CREATE
drops its reference, the tree can be freed while the published file still
points to it.

Mark and remove the tree connection before closing its files, and serialize
both new-open and durable-reconnect volatile ID publication with that state
transition. An opener is then either published in time for the close pass
or rejected after disconnect with STATUS_NETWORK_NAME_DELETED.

Keep a tree reference while a file carries its tree pointer. This protects
asynchronous users that can defer the file's final destruction past tree
disconnect.

The close pass can race the successful FP_NEW to FP_INITED transition.
Take the opening request's file reference atomically with that transition.
This keeps the file alive until request completion even if teardown removes
the ID immediately.

  Read of size 4 at addr ff11000101540f80 by task poc/153

  Call Trace:
    proc_show_files (fs/smb/server/vfs_cache.c:126)
    seq_read_iter (fs/seq_file.c:231)
    proc_reg_read_iter (fs/proc/inode.c:299)
    vfs_read (fs/read_write.c:574)
    ksys_read (fs/read_write.c:716)
    do_syscall_64 (arch/x86/entry/syscall_64.c:84)
    entry_SYSCALL_64_after_hwframe (arch/x86/entry/entry_64.S:121)

  Allocated by:
    ksmbd_tree_conn_connect (fs/smb/server/mgmt/tree_connect.c:35)
    smb2_tree_connect (fs/smb/server/smb2pdu.c:2819)
    handle_ksmbd_work (fs/smb/server/server.c:368)

  Freed by:
    kfree (mm/slub.c:6801)
    handle_ksmbd_work (fs/smb/server/server.c:332)

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: L2CAP: Only accept connection responses to outstanding requests

An outgoing channel waits in BT_CONNECT until security
and the feature mask exchange complete, and only then
sends its connection request. A peer can answer it
before that with a connection response matching our
source CID. The channel then moves to BT_CONFIG,
completes configuration and becomes connected before
security has completed. If security then fails,
l2cap_security_cfm() leaves the connected channel
alone, so it stays up on a link that did not reach
the required security level.

A connection response with a zero source CID is
matched by identifier. Another channel can hold the
same identifier for a response it still has to send,
so the lookup can pick the wrong channel.

Only accept a connection response while our request
is outstanding, and only look at such channels when
matching by identifier.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

Bluetooth: L2CAP: Reject signalling responses in invalid states

A peer can send configuration messages while an
incoming channel is in BT_CONNECT2, before the
security or deferred accept gate has completed. A
configuration response can then promote the channel
to BT_CONNECTED. Configuration responses can also
act on channels that are closing, and a late connection
response can move a disconnecting channel back to
BT_CONFIG.

Accept connection responses only while waiting in
BT_CONNECT. Answer configuration requests in
BT_CONNECT2, but defer our own request until
BT_CONFIG so configuration cannot complete before
the gate. Ignore configuration responses outside
BT_CONFIG and BT_CONNECTED, and only complete
configuration in BT_CONFIG.

In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

cxl/features: Ensure that count is set before access to ent[] __counted_by()

get_supported_features() assigns entries->num_features only after the
memcpy() loop that fills entries->ent[] has already run. Since ent[]
is __counted_by(num_features), the compiler's bounds instrumentation
sees a 0-length array during that loop and FORTIFY_SOURCE trips on
the memcpy. Set @num_features right after allocation, before any
write into ent[], so the bound is correct for the whole lifetime of
the array.

This was found via a fortify panic:

 memcpy: detected buffer overflow: 384 byte write of buffer size 0
 WARNING: lib/string_helpers.c:1035 at __fortify_report+0x54/0xa0
 kernel BUG at lib/string_helpers.c:1043!
 Call trace:
  __fortify_panic+0x10/0x18
  get_supported_features.isra.0+0x4a0/0x4d0 [cxl_core]
  devm_cxl_setup_features+0x84/0x120 [cxl_core]
  cxl_pci_probe+0x254/0x5e0 [cxl_pci]

Same class of bug, same fix shape as commit 6c9d2e87df40
("cxl/fwctl: Fix __fortify_panic"), which fixed the analogous issue
in cxlctl_get_supported_features() but missed this one.

A flaw was found in the Kuadrant WebAssembly (WASM) shim shipped in Red Hat Connectivity Link 1.5. When a TokenRateLimitPolicy is attached to an HTTPRoute that also has an AuthPolicy - or when a RateLimitPolicy with defaults or overrides is attached to the Gateway or listener of such routes - the shim's action pipeline fails to dispatch the authentication guard at request time, and the request is forwarded upstream. Unauthenticated requests return 200 OK instead of 401, and neither authentication nor rate limiting is enforced. Both policies continue to report Enforced, leaving no status-level indication of the failure.

The Toocheke Companion plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Missing Authorization leading to arbitrary post and attachment deletion in versions up to, and including, 2.38. This is due to a missing object-level capability check in the toocheke_tapas_ajax_cleanup_start() and toocheke_tapas_ajax_cleanup_step() AJAX handlers; the toocheke_tapas_cleanup_ajax_guard() method only verifies the primitive delete_posts capability (held by every Contributor) and never calls current_user_can('delete_post', $post_id) or delete_others_posts before passing the attacker-supplied series_post_id to wp_delete_post() and wp_delete_attachment() with force-delete enabled. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with Contributor-level access and above, to permanently delete any importer-created series post, every child 'comic' post attached to it, and every Media Library attachment belonging to those posts — regardless of which user originally created them.

The rtMedia for WordPress, BuddyPress and bbPress plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to generic SQL Injection via the 'custom_fields' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 4.7.17 due to insufficient escaping on the user supplied parameter and lack of sufficient preparation on the existing SQL query. The WPZOOM Forms – Drag & Drop Contact Form Builder for WordPress plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to authorization bypass in all versions up to, and including, 2.0.12 This is due to the plugin not properly verifying that a user is authorized to perform an action. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to view the Name, Email address, and message excerpt stored in the _wpzf_fields meta of every form submission site-wide, regardless of submission ownership. Because public form submissions are stored with post_author=0, WordPress's built-in author-scoping guard in WP_Posts_List_Table is bypassed for Contributors who own zero submissions, causing the list query to return all submissions site-wide rather than only the authenticated user's own records.

The Mail Mint – Email Marketing, Automation & WooCommerce Emails with AI Assistance plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'form_id' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 1.31.9 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. A crafted form_id value such as `1" onmouseover="alert(1)` still resolves to a valid form ID via FormModel::get()'s %d prepared statement placeholder, allowing the payload to bypass empty/draft early-return guards and reach both the HTML id and hidden input value attribute sinks.

The UiChemy – Convert Figma, Prompts and AI Builds to Elementor, Gutenberg and Bricks plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Stored Cross-Site Scripting via the 'sections[0][settings][raw_css]' parameter in all versions up to, and including, 5.5.3 due to insufficient input sanitization and output escaping. This makes it possible for authenticated attackers, with contributor-level access and above, to inject arbitrary web scripts in pages that will execute whenever a user accesses an injected page. The sanitizer bypass relies on HTML entity-encoding the CSS breakout payload at save time, which passes the byte-based filter unchanged and is later reconstituted into executable markup by the render-time html_entity_decode call.

Validating an untrusted ISO 8601 duration string into a timedelta field with Pydantic V1 takes quadratic time: an input of a few dozen kilobytes takes seconds to validate.

The iso8601_duration_re regular expression used to parse ISO 8601 durations (in pydantic/datetime_parse.py) contains an unescaped ".", which also matches digits. On a string of digits, the repeated groups overlap and the regex engine backtracks in quadratic time.

The issue was fixed in commit 62791e66a9f8f118e465ed760c9e2ede9ae3055e. Users relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2 should upgrade to 2.14.2 or later.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into timedelta fields.

Validating an untrusted list into a field constrained with unique_items=True with Pydantic V1 takes quadratic time: an input of a few hundred kilobytes takes seconds to validate.

The ConstrainedList.unique_items_validator validator (in pydantic/types.py) checks each item against all the following ones. For a list with no duplicates (the common, valid case), this results in a quadratic number of comparisons.

The issue was fixed in commit 6ec75e57f277a820ec583e601167f25fe8dc7c87. Users relying on the pydantic.v1 namespace in Pydantic V2 should upgrade to 2.14.2 or later.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted lists into fields constrained with unique_items=True (using conlist() or Field()).

The fix only applies to lists of builtin scalar types (int, float, str, bytes, bool and None), for which duplicates can be detected in linear time. Lists of other types (e.g. models or dictionaries) are still checked in quadratic time, as their items aren't guaranteed to be hashable: bound their size using the max_items constraint.

Pydantic V2 models are not affected.

When extra data is allowed, providing both the alias and the name of an aliased TypedDict or dataclass field makes the unvalidated value (provided under the name) overwrite the validated one (provided under the alias), resulting in validated data not matching the declared type.

Extra items are stored in the same dictionary as the fields (the returned dictionary for TypedDict, the instance __dict__ for dataclasses). As only the alias is marked as used, the field name is treated as an extra item, and its unvalidated value overrides the validated one. The TypedDict validator (pydantic-core/src/validators/typed_dict.rs) and the dataclass validator (pydantic-core/src/validators/dataclass.rs) share this logic.

The issue was fixed in commit 34491f5328f168f14e3769cd5f0f83c0af0f4778.

Impact: validation bypass, as data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted data into TypedDict or dataclass types with aliased fields and extra data allowed (with extra='allow', or with the extra_items argument for TypedDict), using Pydantic V2 (up to and including 2.14.1).

Pydantic models (BaseModel) are not affected, as extra data is stored separately from fields.

Validating an untrusted string in exponent notation into a Fraction field computes the full power of ten without any bound: an input of a few bytes takes seconds to validate.

String inputs are passed to the Fraction constructor. For strings in exponent notation (e.g. '1e8000000'), CPython computes the corresponding power of ten as an integer (in Lib/fractions.py).

The issue was fixed in commit 69ed168e9ad465eef4c8d81efb152a93b604daf5. For strings in exponent notation, the exponent is now parsed before calling the Fraction constructor, and exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into Fraction fields (in both JSON and Python mode, including in strict mode), using Pydantic from 2.10.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.0.

From 2.14.0, exponents larger than 4300 (in absolute value) are rejected, matching the maximum number of digits accepted for integers.

Validating an untrusted URL with a long scheme and many hosts into a multi-host URL field (e.g. PostgresDsn) takes quadratic time and memory: an input of about a hundred kilobytes takes around a gigabyte of memory to validate.

The parse_multihost_url() function (in pydantic-core/src/validators/url.rs) parses each host separately, prepending the whole URL prefix (including the scheme) to every one of them. As the scheme can be arbitrarily long, and is parsed and stored once per host, both time and memory grow quadratically with the input size. Allowed schemes (e.g. postgres for PostgresDsn) are only checked after parsing, so they don't prevent the issue.

The issue was fixed in commit b4028f9d87e34750e53be0ba011d70f3c0fcc94e.

Impact: denial of service through validation of untrusted input. Affected are applications validating untrusted strings into multi-host URL fields (PostgresDsn, MongoDsn, NatsDsn, or custom types built on MultiHostUrl).

When validating JSON data into a model allowing extra data, the keys of extra data aren't validated against the key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__, resulting in extra data not matching the declared type. This is the case if you define __pydantic_extra__ as e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=r'^x_')], int].

The validate_json_by_iteration() method (in pydantic-core/src/validators/model_fields.rs), used to validate JSON data into models, only validates the values of extra data, and stores the keys as is.

The issue was fixed in commit 4c65dbda9970a488e2ff21c8693fc6f6d70a3358.

Impact: validation bypass, as extra data returned by validation doesn't match the declared type. Affected are applications validating untrusted JSON data into models allowing extra data (with extra='allow'), with a key type annotated on __pydantic_extra__ (e.g. dict[Annotated[str, Field(pattern=...)], int]), using Pydantic from 2.13.0 up to (but excluding) 2.14.2.

Python mode validation isn't affected.

When message history is serialized and loaded again, a tool result that contains a JSON object in the serialized shape of one of Pydantic AI's file types is rebuilt as that file. A third party who controls data a tool returns, such as a record that an MCP server or a function tool returns from an external system, can use this to make the application download a URL on its local network, or make the model provider read an s3:// object or uploaded file with the application's credentials. Applications are affected when tool results can contain third-party data, message history containing those results is serialized and loaded again (stored history, history a UI adapter holds on the server, or Temporal, DBOS or Prefect durable execution), and the model is one Pydantic AI downloads files for, one that honors force_download, or one whose provider resolves non-HTTP file URLs or uploaded files. History that a client submits through the Vercel AI or AG-UI adapter in the default mode is not affected. The issue is fixed in pydantic-ai and pydantic-ai-slim 1.107.10 and 2.66.0.

vulnerability-lookup prior to version 7.1.0 contains two security issues in its web interface. First, the /user/toggle_2fa endpoint accepted HTTP GET requests and disabled the authenticated user's two-factor authentication without requiring password confirmation. Because the state-changing operation was reachable via GET, an attacker with a basic account could embed an image element (or any other GET-triggering markup) in a comment pointing to that endpoint. When a victim with 2FA enabled viewed the comment, their browser silently issued the GET request, disabling the victim's second factor of authentication. No CSRF token was enforced on the GET path, and no password was required to confirm the action. Second, the comment detail page (/comment/<uuid>) rendered unpublished comments to any visitor who possessed the URL, bypassing the moderation workflow that was intended to keep such content hidden until approved. The API correctly restricted access, but the web view did not enforce the same authorization check. The combined effect allows an attacker to degrade a victim's account security (removal of 2FA) through a single page view and to read content that was not yet approved for public release.

Flowintel's community data launcher script passes the admin API key as a command-line argument to a child Python helper process. On Unix-like systems, process arguments are readable by all local users via standard tools such as ps or by reading /proc/<pid>/cmdline, allowing any local user to observe the key while the helper process is running.

An attacker with local access to the host can capture the admin API key during the brief window in which the helper process is active. Possession of the key grants full administrative access to the Flowintel REST API, enabling unauthorized creation, modification, or deletion of threat intelligence data, users, roles, and organisations.

Preconditions:
- The victim must invoke the community data import or deletion command (launch.sh -tdc or -dtdc) with the API key supplied as a positional argument.
- The attacker must have a local user account on the same host and be able to observe process listings during the helper execution window.

Impact:
- Disclosure of the Flowintel admin API key to any local user.
- Subsequent full administrative control over the Flowintel instance via its REST API.

Affected: <4.1.0
